blinding_guess.why: All seven packet elements are the visual meshes, and all seven are binary STL files whose 80-byte header begins with the ASCII keyword 'solid' (e.g. 'solid Base', 'solid L-Axis') with no 'endsolid'; STL readers that sniff 'solid' as ASCII (e.g. the RViz mesh loader) warn about or mis-detect such files. The collision meshes, not in the packet, use 'Exported from Blender-2.69' headers. The visual files also carry executable mode bits. Either could be what a later revision changes; the geometry itself looks sane (metre-scale extents).

notes: Resource elements have no declares template in the instructions; I used the pattern of the other templates, 'resource <uri>: <format>', with the format taken from the URI extension ('stl'), and put byte size, facet count, header text and raw-byte sha256 in provenance. definition_id is null for every port: an STL mesh is not a msg/srv/action/idl definition, and definition_hash.py sha256 normalises text, which does not apply to a binary file. msg_type, QoS and rates are null: these are file resources, not topics, and the package is ROS 1. frame is the link each visual mesh is attached to in the xacro macro (the source loaded by launch/load_mh5.launch:3 via urdf/mh5.xacro), written with its ${prefix} as in code. units null: the URDF <mesh> elements set no scale attribute and the code states no unit; vertex extents are metre-scale (e.g. MH5_L_AXIS.stl z 0 to 0.38 vs joint_u offset 0.3100, MH5_R_AXIS.stl x 0 to 0.2695 vs joint_b offset 0.2335) and match the collision meshes to within about 0.1 mm. Header detail: every visual STL is structurally binary (file size = 84 + 50*facet count; facets parse with no NaN/Inf) but its header starts with 'solid ' padded with spaces, and the files contain no 'endsolid'. Mode detail: meshes/mh5/visual/*.stl are -rwxr-xr-x in the snapshot; meshes/mh5/collision/*.stl are -rw-r--r--.
